title: Modi Was Personally Invited to Khamenei's Funeral. India Sent a Deputy Minister Instead.
excerpt: As Iran stages a week of mass processions for its slain Supreme Leader, India's carefully calibrated delegation reveals the diplomatic tightrope New Delhi walks between Tehran and Washington.
body:
Iran's president personally invited Narendra Modi. India sent a deputy foreign minister instead.

As the body of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei lay in state at Tehran's Grand Mosalla mosque on Friday — the start of what Iran is billing as one of the largest funeral processions in modern history — New Delhi's choice of delegation told its own quiet story about the diplomatic tightrope India walks between Tehran and Washington.

India announced Thursday that Deputy Foreign Minister Pabitra Margherita and Bihar Governor Lt. Gen. (Retd) Syed Ata Hasnain would represent the country at the week-long funeral ceremonies. The foreign ministry framed it as "high-level representation" that "underscores the importance of civilizational ties, including people-to-people connection, between the two countries."

The diplomatic community read it differently. India sent enough to honour an ancient relationship. Not enough to alarm its closest strategic partners.

## A Careful Calibration

Khamenei, who ruled Iran for 37 years, was killed on February 28 — the first day of the U.S.-Israeli military campaign that devastated Iran's military infrastructure and plunged the Gulf into its worst crisis in decades. His funeral, postponed for months due to the ongoing war, has become as much a geopolitical event as a religious one.

Iran says it expects representatives from 100 countries. The dignitaries who filed past Khamenei's coffin on Friday included Russia's Dmitry Medvedev, China's He Wei, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, and Pakistan's powerful army chief Asif Munir. But as one analyst noted, "No major power is sending its top leader."

India's delegation fell squarely in this pattern. Modi was personally invited by Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian — a gesture that carried significant weight given India's strategic importance to Tehran. But attending would have complicated India's deepening defence and technology partnerships with both the United States and Israel, the two countries that carried out the strike that killed Khamenei.

## Political Figures Walked Their Own Line

In a notable twist, Iran extended separate invitations to India's political parties. BJP National President Nitin Nabin and Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge both received formal invitations, as did Congress foreign affairs chair Salman Khurshid.

First visuals from Tehran on Friday showed former Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Mehbooba Mufti and Salman Khurshid among the Indian attendees, alongside several religious leaders. Their presence — in a personal capacity, distinct from the official government delegation — allowed India to maintain multiple channels of engagement without elevating the government's own representation.

It was a characteristically Indian solution: present on every frequency, committed on none.

## What's at Stake Between India and Iran

The relationship between New Delhi and Tehran runs deeper than any single funeral. India has significant strategic and economic interests tied to Iran that cannot be easily set aside:

**Chabahar Port**, India's flagship connectivity project in southeastern Iran, remains the country's only viable route to Afghanistan and Central Asia that bypasses Pakistan. The port has faced years of uncertainty due to U.S. sanctions but has seen renewed activity after the interim U.S.-Iran ceasefire agreement.

**Energy security** is another factor. India was once among Iran's largest oil customers before halting purchases under U.S. sanctions pressure in 2019. With the U.S. now easing some sanctions on Iranian oil sales as part of its push for a final peace deal, India may see an opportunity to diversify its crude sources — particularly as it recalibrates supply chains away from its earlier reliance on Russian oil during the Gulf conflict.

**The Strait of Hormuz**, through which roughly one-fifth of the world's oil flows, remains a live flashpoint. India, as one of the world's largest oil importers, has an outsized stake in the ongoing U.S.-Iran negotiations over freedom of navigation. The funeral has effectively paused those talks — Qatar's foreign ministry said negotiations would resume after Khamenei's burial on July 9.

## The Broader Diplomatic Picture

India's approach to the Khamenei funeral fits a pattern that has defined its foreign policy throughout the Gulf crisis: maintaining relationships with all sides while avoiding the appearance of alignment with any single camp.

New Delhi has deepened its defence ties with the United States throughout 2026 — from joint military exercises to semiconductor partnerships. It has simultaneously maintained dialogue with Iran through BRICS, where India holds the 2026 presidency, and through bilateral engagement on Chabahar and the International North-South Transport Corridor.

The funeral delegation was calibrated to that exact frequency. A retired military officer as governor (Ata Hasnain's background signals respect for Iran's sovereignty and sacrifice without political overtones), and a deputy foreign minister (senior enough to be taken seriously, junior enough to avoid headlines).

## Why the Diaspora Should Watch This Space

For NRIs in the United States and the Gulf, the India-Iran relationship has direct implications. The Strait of Hormuz negotiations will determine oil prices and shipping routes that affect everything from petrol costs to the price of goods imported by Indian businesses in the UAE and Saudi Arabia.

The broader question of how India navigates between its Western partnerships and its historical non-aligned instincts will shape everything from visa policies to trade deals to the diaspora's own positioning in their adopted countries' political conversations.

India's message from Tehran this week was unmistakable: we are here, but we are not choosing sides. Whether that tightrope can hold through the rest of 2026 remains an open question.
